flashcards.q: What is the weak generational hypothesis and why does it make young GC cheap?
flashcards.a: Most objects die shortly after allocation. A young GC only scans the young generation plus a remembered set of old->young references, not the whole heap, so cost scales with live young-gen data, not total heap size.

flashcards.q: What is a G1 humongous object and why does it cause more Full GCs than the live data size suggests?
flashcards.a: Any object larger than 50% of the region size. It's allocated directly into contiguous regions, bypassing the cheap young-gen lifecycle -- behaves as old-gen data from allocation, reclaimable only via old/mixed collection, fragmenting the heap.

flashcards.q: What does -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis actually control, and what's its default?
flashcards.a: A soft TARGET (not a guarantee), default 200ms. G1 sizes young-gen and mixed-GC work to try to hit it; setting it unrealistically low increases GC frequency sharply rather than guaranteeing shorter pauses.

flashcards.q: What specific failure mode killed CMS, and what's its G1 analog?
flashcards.a: CMS never compacted concurrently, so old gen fragmented until a large allocation had no contiguous space, forcing a full stop-the-world compaction ('concurrent mode failure'). G1's analog: allocation outpacing concurrent marking triggers a Full GC fallback -- same lineage, concurrent collector falling behind.

flashcards.q: Mechanically, how does ZGC achieve sub-millisecond pauses regardless of heap size?
flashcards.a: Colored pointers encode object state in unused pointer bits; every reference read goes through a load barrier that transparently fixes a stale reference if the object moved. Relocation happens concurrently with the app running, so the stop-the-world component shrinks to small, heap-size-independent bookkeeping.

flashcards.q: What's ZGC's real, permanent cost versus G1?
flashcards.a: 15-30% more memory, 5-10% more CPU for equivalent workloads -- the structural price of concurrent relocation, not a tuning artifact.

flashcards.q: When did Generational ZGC become the default, and what happened to non-generational ZGC?
flashcards.a: Default since JDK 23 (JEP 474). Non-generational mode was later removed entirely (JEP 490) because generational mode won essentially every benchmark, cutting CPU overhead ~30-40% on allocation-heavy workloads.

flashcards.q: List the JIT tiers from cold to hot.
flashcards.a: Tier 0 interpreter -> Tier 1 C1 no profiling -> Tier 2/3 C1 with increasing profiling -> Tier 4 C2 full optimization (inlining, loop unrolling, escape analysis).

flashcards.q: Why is a naive 'time it in a loop' Java microbenchmark unreliable?
flashcards.a: It includes interpreter and C1 warm-up phases in the measurement, so for anything but very large N it measures compilation behavior, not steady-state C2-optimized throughput. Use JMH with a discarded warm-up phase.

flashcards.q: What causes JIT deoptimization, and what's the observable symptom of a method thrashing on it?
flashcards.a: C2 compiled code based on an optimistic assumption (e.g. monomorphic call site) that later proves wrong when a second implementation appears; the JVM falls back to the interpreter and recompiles. Symptom: the same method repeatedly compiled/discarded/recompiled, visible via JFR jdk.Deoptimization events or -XX:+PrintCompilation.

flashcards.q: In a G1 GC log line, what does a shrinking before->after heap-used gap over many collections (with flat traffic) indicate?
flashcards.a: A slow memory leak -- less garbage is reclaimed each cycle because more objects stay permanently live. Fix with a heap dump and retained-size analysis, not GC flag tuning.

flashcards.q: What does async-profiler see that JFR misses, and vice versa?
flashcards.a: async-profiler samples via perf_events/AsyncGetCallTrace outside JVM instrumentation, so it sees native frames (JNI, native libs) JFR misses. JFR is always-on-capable at <1% overhead and correlates GC/allocation/deopt/thread events on one shared timeline in a single recording -- complementary tools, not either/or.
